question: Why is the speaker renowned as the supreme person in both world and Veda?
premises: Because I transcend the perishable and even the imperishable, I am supreme.
Therefore I am renowned in the world and in the Veda as the supreme person.
The text says that in the world there are these two persons.
Even with unawakened nature, all know the conscious self with a body made of elements as perishable form, from the world's delusion, so the dualistic view does not cease.
But I, all-gracious, split the dualistic knot and, pervading all the world, am to be known.
I transcend the perishable because beings are inert, and the imperishable because all-pervasion is denied in the unawakened self.
Thus by explanations beginning with the supreme person in world and Veda, he alone is said to be the supreme nondual self.
inference: The supreme person is not merely beyond perishable and imperishable forms but is the all-pervading nondual self to be known after the dualistic knot is split.
uncertainties: The fused compound glosses and hyphenated editorial readings make some clause boundaries interpretive rather than strictly separable.
plain_english: Because I transcend both the perishable and the imperishable, I am supreme; therefore I am renowned in the world and in the Veda as the supreme person. The text says there are these two persons in the world. Even in an unawakened state, people know the conscious self with a body made of elements as perishable form, and from the world's delusion the dualistic view does not cease. But I, all-gracious, split the dualistic knot and, pervading all the world, am to be known. I transcend the perishable because beings are inert, and the imperishable because all-pervasion is denied in the unawakened self. Thus, by explanations beginning with the supreme person in world and Veda, he alone is said to be the supreme nondual self.
